title: Too young (Jeremiah 1:4–10)
hook: I'm only a child, says Jeremiah; before you were born I knew you

segments.voice: Yesterday, good news to the poor, and your line was beauty for ashes. Who did you show up for? Day four hundred seventy-three.

First day at a new job. Everyone else seems to know what they're doing. Someone hands you a task that feels three sizes too big, and the voice in your head is instant: I'm not ready. I'm too new. Somebody older should do this. Now leave Isaiah behind and meet the next prophet. Jeremiah comes from a family of priests in Anathoth, a village in the land of Benjamin. The book says God's word came to him in the thirteenth year of King Josiah. He's going to spend the rest of his working life, through king after king, telling powerful people what they don't want to hear. And his very first answer to God is that voice. Today, the prophet who said he was too young.
screen: `FIRST DAY. A TASK TOO BIG.` → `I'M NOT READY.` → `JEREMIAH OF ANATHOTH.`

segments.voice: God speaks first, in the King James Bible: "Before I formed thee in the belly I knew thee; and before thou camest forth out of the womb I sanctified thee, and I ordained thee a prophet unto the nations." Knew, in Hebrew, can mean more than having information: the knowing of close relationship, even of choosing. Sanctified means set apart. Before he had a single skill, before he'd said a word, he was known. And Jeremiah answers: "Ah, Lord GOD! behold, I cannot speak: for I am a child." The Hebrew word is na'ar. It can mean a boy, or a young man, a teenager or someone in his early twenties. The text never gives his age. What it gives is his answer: too young, not a speaker, not enough. Notice that God doesn't argue. He doesn't say you're older than you think, or you're actually a gifted speaker. He says: "Say not, I am a child: for thou shalt go to all that I shall send thee, and whatsoever I command thee thou shalt speak." And then, be not afraid, for I am with you. Then the Lord reaches out and touches Jeremiah's mouth: "Behold, I have put my words in thy mouth." Like Isaiah's coal, the call goes to the lips, the very place he felt weakest. The answer to I'm not enough isn't you are enough. It's I will be with you. Christians often read this call as a word to anyone who feels too small for what's in front of them, and some hear verse five as a sign that God knows each person before birth.
screen: `BEFORE I FORMED THEE, I KNEW THEE.` · `NA'AR: A BOY, A YOUNG MAN.` · `GOD DOESN'T ARGUE: I AM WITH YOU.` · `WORDS PUT IN HIS MOUTH.` · then, large: `SAY NOT, I AM A CHILD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find one thing you feel too small for. Settle, and breathe. Name it: a conversation you've been avoiding, a job you don't think you're qualified for, a gift you haven't used, a step you keep saying you'll take someday. Notice the excuse that comes with it. Too young. Too old. Not good with words. Not the type. Then picture the first small step of it, just the first. Not the whole thing. If you pray, you can hold it before God with Jeremiah's honest words: I cannot speak. Then listen. The bell holds the time.
Too young. Jeremiah's first answer to God, I am a child, and God's reply: say not so; I am with you.
Your line: before you were born. Today, do the first small step of the thing you feel too small for. Just the first. Day four hundred seventy-three.

howItsDone: Jeremiah 1:4–10 is read at ordinations and services of commissioning, and is often given to young people in churches as a reminder that their age doesn't disqualify them from serving God.

original.note: Hebrew: a boy, a youth, a young man. it doesn't fix an age.

trapdoor: what you thought: Jeremiah was a little kid.
what it means: a young man who felt too young and unskilled, told that God knew him first and would go with him.
what a scholar hears: na'ar covers a wide age range. the book dates the call by a king, Josiah's thirteenth year, and runs it to the day Jerusalem's people were carried away.

notes: Josiah's 13th year (Jeremiah 1:2) commonly dated c. 627/626 BC; 'forty years' of ministry (to the fall of Jerusalem in 587/586 and after) is an approximation. Confirm.
Trapdoor: 'Jeremiah is the longest book in the Bible by word count' (Hebrew). Commonly stated; Psalms has more chapters. Confirm or remove.
Jeremiah 1:5 is also cited in modern debates about the unborn; the script mentions only that 'God knows each person before birth' without entering that debate. Keeper may prefer to omit.
